content: Erythema toxicum is a highly prevalent rash observed in newborn infants. It occurs in up to 50% of full-term neonates, typically manifesting between the second and fifth day after birth. The rash is characterized by small pustular lesions, each situated on an individual reddened base. In some cases, the appearance of the rash may raise concerns about herpes simplex infection. However, herpes simplex lesions generally present with a more clustered and vesicular morphology. When the diagnosis is uncertain, a scraping of a lesion can be performed, and the fluid can be examined microscopically. Herpes lesions will yield a positive result on a direct fluorescent antibody test, whereas the fluid from erythema toxicum lesions will reveal a predominance of eosinophils. The exact cause of erythema toxicum remains unknown. However, it is considered a benign condition that does not cause discomfort to the infant. The rash typically resolves spontaneously within approximately two weeks.
